summary:
ASTROSAGE is an offline-first Astronaut Health Intelligence and Protocol Copilot developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 challenge, “Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions.”

The platform brings together astronaut physiological health records, personal baselines, environmental observations, radiation exposure records, reported symptoms, and mission events into a unified health timeline. Its monitoring module helps identify deviations from personal baselines through visual trends and explainable flags.

ASTROSAGE also features a local AI-powered Copilot that retrieves information from locally stored scientific references and provides evidence-supported explanations, designed to remain accessible without internet connectivity.

By combining health monitoring, mission context, and offline scientific knowledge retrieval, ASTROSAGE aims to support informed health awareness and structured reporting for human medical review during long-duration space missions. The prototype uses simulated demonstration data and is not a clinically validated medical system.
details: ASTROSAGE is designed as an offline-first astronaut health intelligence platform that brings health monitoring, mission context and scientific knowledge retrieval into one system. 1. THE PROBLEM During long-duration space missions, astronauts operate in environments involving microgravity, radiation exposure, isolation and communication constraints. Monitoring changes in individual health and accessing relevant medical knowledge can be challenging when continuous connectivity to Earth cannot be assumed. 2. OUR SOLUTION ASTROSAGE consists of two integrated modules: A. ASTROSAGE MONITOR • Organizes physiological health measurements and personal baseline records. • Visualizes health trends and changes over a mission timeline. • Displays explainable monitoring flags when readings deviate from configured baselines. • Brings together radiation exposure records, environmental observations, reported symptoms and mission events. • Helps identify missing or incomplete records to support better data awareness. B. ASTROSAGE COPILOT • Uses a locally available AI model to assist with scientific information retrieval. • Searches locally stored scientific reference documents. • Generates evidence-supported explanations with source references. • Is designed to provide access to its local knowledge base without depending on an active internet connection. 3. SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE Health and mission records are organized, validated and stored locally. An analytics layer processes the records to produce trends, timelines and monitoring flags for the dashboard. For scientific knowledge retrieval, local reference documents are converted into searchable representations. A vector retrieval system retrieves relevant passages, which are provided to the local AI model to generate source-supported responses. 4. TECHNOLOGY The proposed development stack includes a React and TypeScript frontend, Python and FastAPI backend, SQLite for local storage, data-processing libraries, and a local AI retrieval pipeline using Ollama, Sentence Transformers and FAISS. Only technologies actually implemented in the submitted prototype should be considered part of the final implementation. 5. INNOVATION AND IMPACT ASTROSAGE combines personal-baseline monitoring, mission-context visualization and offline scientific knowledge retrieval in one workflow. Its focus is not simply displaying measurements, but helping users understand changes, inspect supporting references and prepare structured information for human medical review. 6. VALIDATION AND RESPONSIBLE USE The demonstration uses simulated astronaut health records and fictional mission scenarios. These are not real NASA telemetry or clinical measurements. ASTROSAGE is an experimental prototype, not a NASA-approved or clinically validated medical system. Its monitoring flags are informational and do not establish diagnoses or prove that one exposure caused a health change. Medical decisions require qualified human review. FUTURE DEVELOPMENT Future work could include integration with validated spaceflight datasets, approved health-monitoring devices, expert-reviewed protocols and more extensive testing under realistic mission scenarios.
